context: An-Najm is Makkan and answers one charge in particular, that the Prophet ﷺ was producing the Qur'an out of his own inclination. Its first answer is testimony rather than argument: your companion has not strayed and does not speak from desire, and what he brought is revelation. It then describes what he saw, twice, insisting each time on the accuracy of the seeing rather than its grandeur.

Since the charge concerned invention, the second half turns to invention of another kind. The three goddesses of Makkah are named and then reduced to words: they are names you have named, you and your fathers, with no authority sent down. That opposition sets the shape: revelation on one side, inherited naming on the other.
name_story: The surah is named for the star of its first verse, sworn by as it descends. Commentators differed over what the star is, some reading a particular star and others reading the Qur'an itself as it came down in portions. Either reading suits a surah about something arriving from above and a man who reported it exactly.

movements.note: The Prophet ﷺ is defended in three clauses: not astray, not speaking from desire, only conveying revelation. The one of great power approaches to within two bow lengths, and a second sighting is placed at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary.
Al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat are named, and the argument against them is not that they are weak but that they are empty, names handed down by fathers.
Those who call the angels by female names are following conjecture, which avails nothing against truth, and the stretch ends by forbidding people to declare themselves pure.
A man who gave a little and then stopped is referred to the scrolls of Musa and of Ibrahim, which are quoted: no bearer bears another's burden, and man has nothing except what he strove for.
Short clauses assign to Allah what people assign elsewhere: laughter and weeping, death and life, the two mates from a drop, wealth and what suffices, the lordship of Sirius.

This is a warner of the same kind as the warners of old, and the Approaching Day has drawn near. The surah describes an audience that laughs instead of weeping, then drops the argument for a command to prostrate and worship.

themes.d: The surah defends the Prophet ﷺ as a witness and not an author, and its wording is about seeing and about whether the eye and the heart reported accurately. Who was seen has been disputed since the first generation: most commentators read verses 5 to 10 as Jibril, Aisha denied that he saw his Lord, and a different view is reported from Ibn Abbas.
The three goddesses and the female-named angels are treated as one error, a word inherited and repeated until it seemed to refer to something real.
That nobody carries another's load and that a person receives what he worked for are quoted from the oldest scriptures the surah names, presented as ancient rather than new.

themes.t: An ending that is an action
themes.d: The surah does not finish with a summary or a threat. It finishes with a command to prostrate and worship, which is why its recitation has always carried a prostration at the last verse.

heart: The first eighteen verses are among the few places in the Qur'an that describe what happened to the Prophet ﷺ himself, and on a slow reading their restraint is the thing to notice. Almost nothing is described. There is a distance, a covering that covered, a tree, and a repeated insistence that the sight was exact. What is preserved is the reliability of the witness rather than the vision itself.

The second half changes its subject to the reader without announcing it. Verse 32 forbids anyone to declare his own purity and mentions the womb in the same breath, dating a person's record earlier than any achievement he could cite. Verses 38 and 39 then remove every borrowed merit and leave a man holding only what he worked at.

passages.why: The denial that he speaks from desire, followed by the statement that it is revelation revealed: the surah's central claim in two short verses.
Idols reduced to names that people invented and then inherited. The method, attacking the word rather than the statue, is worth sitting with.
The prohibition on claiming purity for oneself, grounded in Allah's knowledge of a person from before he was born.
No bearer of burdens bears the burden of another, and man has nothing but what he strove for, quoted from the scriptures of Musa and Ibrahim.

connections.why: Al-Isra states the night travel to the Farthest Mosque in one verse, and An-Najm gives the sighting at the Lote Tree: together the two accounts a reader has.
At-Takwir also defends the Prophet ﷺ against the charge of madness and states that he saw the messenger on the clear horizon, in a different vocabulary.

virtue.text: An authentic prophetic practice is attached to this surah, not a merit promised to the reciter. Ibn Mas'ud reported that the Prophet ﷺ recited An-Najm and prostrated at its end, and that everyone present prostrated with him except one man who took a handful of dust and raised it to his face; the report is in Bukhari and Muslim. The schools differ on the recitation prostration generally, the Hanafis holding it obligatory and the others recommended, and that disagreement is not settled here.
virtue.src: prostration report from Ibn Mas'ud in Bukhari and Muslim; no virtue report
